Where it began

Farokh Engineer was born in Bombay in February 1938. As a boy he dreamed of flying aeroplanes rather than keeping wicket, but a love of games ran through the household and cricket won. He learned the finer points at the Dadar Parsi Colony Sporting Club, where the older members taught him and he soon earned a regular place.

One childhood afternoon at the Brabourne Stadium he shouted a greeting to Denis Compton, who was fielding nearby. Compton handed him a piece of chewing gum, and the young Farokh kept it as a treasure for years. He went to Don Bosco High School and Podar College in Matunga, played for Bombay University and the Indian Universities, and joined the Bombay side in 1959.

The player

His first Test came against England at Kanpur in December 1961. Coming in at number nine, he made 33 in a stand of 53 with Polly Umrigar, then took his first catch behind the stumps to see off Peter Richardson. For the next few years he and Budhi Kunderan shared the gloves, a contest that lasted until Kunderan retired in 1967.

In all he played 46 Tests for India up to 1975, usually opening the batting as well as keeping wicket. He made 2,611 runs at 31.08, with two hundreds, a best of 121 and 16 fifties, and held 66 catches with 16 stumpings. At the 1975 World Cup he made 54 not out against East Africa and became the first man to be named player of the match for India at the tournament.

What made him special

Few keepers have been asked to do so much. Taking every ball behind the stumps and then walking out to face the new one is a hard double, and he did it across 46 Tests. The world noticed too: he was first-choice keeper for the Rest of the World sides led by Garfield Sobers in England in 1970 and in Australia in 1971–72.

When English counties were first allowed overseas players in 1968, Lancashire signed him alongside Clive Lloyd. Over nine seasons the pair helped turn a club without a major trophy since 1950 into a one-day force, collecting four Gillette Cups and two John Player League titles. A keeper who opened the batting rarely had much time to put his feet up.

Away from the middle

He loved life in Manchester and made his home there after he stopped playing, later serving Lancashire as a vice-president. India gave him the Padma Shri, and in January 2024 the BCCI honoured him with its lifetime achievement award named after Colonel C. K. Nayudu. During the England and India Test series for the Anderson–Tendulkar Trophy, a stand was named after him in honour of all he gave Lancashire.

And finally

In the film 83, about India's 1983 World Cup win, he appears as one of the television commentators, played by Boman Irani. It seems fair: a man who spent his career both behind the stumps and in front of them was always going to have plenty to say.
